posts.title: Scaffold dismantling: exclusion zones and controlled lowering after Belfast fatality
posts.excerpt: On 22 October 2026, 7 Towers Scaffolding Ltd was fined £20,000 after a collection driver was fatally struck by a metal scaffold board that fell about 8 m during dismantling on a Belfast site in December 2024. HSENI found the exclusion zone was not adequately controlled so that people not involved in the dismantling could approach. The case reinforces two basic temporary works controls: planned controlled lowering of components, and a physical exclusion zone that keeps everyone else out.
posts.linkedinReady:
On 22 October 2026, 7 Towers Scaffolding Ltd was fined £20,000 at Laganside Crown Court after pleading guilty to a breach of Article 4(1) of the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978.

In December 2024 a collection driver, Samuel Magill, was struck on the head by a metal scaffold board approximately 2.4 m long that fell about 8 m while colleagues were dismantling scaffold on a site on Lisburn Road, Belfast. He died in hospital nearly seven weeks later. HSENI found the company had not adequately controlled the exclusion zone so that people not directly involved in the dismantling could approach the work.

HSENI inspector Kevin Campbell described the incident as entirely preventable. Employers must have robust procedures so that equipment and components are lowered in a controlled method, with clear instructions, and a clearly identified exclusion zone with measures that actually keep unauthorised people out.

This is temporary works management in practice. Scaffold is temporary works. Dismantling is part of the sequence. Collection drivers, other trades, visitors and the public are foreseeable. The Temporary Works Register, the design or TG20 compliance sheet, the assembly/use/dismantling plan, the permit and the competent inspection all need to cover the dismantling phase, not just the working scaffold.

This week:

- Confirm every scaffold has a documented dismantling plan that includes controlled lowering (gin wheel, hoist or equivalent — not throwing) and a physical exclusion zone with marshals or barriers.
- Brief everyone who will be near the scaffold, including drivers and collectors, on the zone and what “keep out” means.
- Treat any change to the sequence or incomplete ties/bracing as a design change until confirmed.

Educational only — not for construction. Subject to the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 22 October 2026, 7 Towers Scaffolding Ltd (County Antrim) was fined £20,000 at Laganside Crown Court after previously pleading guilty to a single breach of Article 4(1) of the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978. On 18 December 2024, while a team was dismantling scaffold on a site on Lisburn Road, Belfast, a metal scaffolding board approximately 2.4 m long became dislodged from the upper part of the structure and fell about 8 m. It struck Samuel Magill, 60, a collection driver employed by the company who had arrived to collect dismantled components. He had parked on the pavement and walked toward the work area. He was struck at the outer edge of the site exclusion zone, next to the pavement. He died in hospital on 5 February 2025.

HSENI found that the company had not sufficiently managed and controlled the exclusion zone around the scaffolding during dismantling, so that people not directly involved in the work could approach. Inspector Kevin Campbell stated the incident was entirely preventable and that employers must ensure robust procedures so equipment and components are lowered to the ground in a controlled method, with clear work instructions communicated to all relevant personnel, and a clear identified exclusion zone with measures to prevent unauthorised persons entering. Scaffold dismantling is a temporary works activity. Falling objects and people entering the drop zone are foreseeable risks under the Work at Height Regulations and CDM 2015. Collection and delivery activity must be planned into the method, not treated as separate.

ul: Every scaffold (including system and tube-and-fitting) is entered on the Temporary Works Register with a named TWC, a design or TG20 compliance sheet, and an assembly, use and dismantling plan that specifically covers striking.
The dismantling plan requires controlled lowering of boards, tubes and fittings (gin wheel, hoist or equivalent). Throwing is not an acceptable method.

A physical exclusion zone is established below the work, clearly signed, and controlled by barriers or marshals so that drivers, other trades, visitors and the public cannot enter. The zone must account for the actual drop path, including items that can bounce or travel beyond the scaffold footprint.

Everyone who will be near the scaffold during dismantling — including collection drivers — is briefed on the zone and the method. A person whose role is to keep others out must not themselves be required to enter the zone.

Ties, bracing and platforms that maintain stability of the remaining scaffold are removed only in the planned sequence. Any departure is treated as a design change until the designer or competent person confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.
A competent person inspects the scaffold before dismantling starts and the permit-to-dismantle (or equivalent) is issued under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: BS 5975-1:2024 requires temporary works, including scaffolding, to be planned, designed (or covered by a standard solution), checked, registered and inspected. NASC TG20:21 and TG30:24 provide recognised configurations and operational guidance that include orderly dismantling from the top, retention of ties as long as possible, and the need for a plan. NASC SG4 addresses the scaffolders’ safe zone during erection and dismantling. HSE HSG150 (Health and safety in construction) addresses exclusion zones and preventing materials falling onto people. Exact clause references should be confirmed against the project’s licensed copies.

This briefing is educational only and is not for construction. It is based on published reports of the prosecution and does not constitute a finding on the specific site. It is subject to project-specific verification, the project temporary works procedure, and acceptance by the competent person (TWC) appointed under that procedure. AI-supported drafting requires competent review before any use on site.

posts.title: Banbury partial collapse: a prompt to re-check temporary stability controls
posts.excerpt: On 21 October a building under construction in Banbury partially collapsed with scaffolding. Two workers were hospitalised. HSE is investigating. Cause is not established. The incident is a prompt to re-confirm temporary works controls on sequence, bracing and load path — the same themes that appear in recent CROSS reports.
posts.linkedinReady:
On 21 October a building under construction on Lower Cherwell Street in Banbury partially collapsed with scaffolding. Nine workers were on site. Two were taken to hospital — one with head and leg injuries, one with severe injuries. HSE is investigating. No cause has been established and none is assumed here.

Incidents like this are a prompt, not a verdict. Structural stability during construction is a temporary-works issue until the permanent structure can stand on its own. Sequence changes, incomplete bracing, unassessed load paths into existing elements, and items treated as “just scaffolding” or “just temporary” sit in the same control space as the CROSS reports that keep appearing.

CROSS-UK Report 1479 (January 2026) is a clear recent example: a late contractor change from lifting beams in pairs to lifting them individually created a lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete that took utilisation over 200% without temporary restraints. The Category II check caught it. Many changes do not.

HSE’s structural stability guidance during alteration, demolition and dismantling is unchanged: temporary supports must be designed, installed and maintained for foreseeable loads, by people competent for the item. BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015 Regulation 19 still require the procedure — design brief, design and check, register, permit and competent inspection — not a verbal “it will be fine”.

Separately, Build UK’s Common Assessment Standard Version 6 (effective 1 November 2026) clarifies that scaffolding and temporary works do not fall within the Building Safety Regulations unless they form part of the completed structure. NASC welcomed the distinction. Competence requirements move, not disappear. The procedural controls under BS 5975 and CDM remain.

This week, for every live item that could affect stability:

- Confirm it is on the Temporary Works Register with a named TWC.
- Ask for the design (or documented standard solution), check category, permit and last competent inspection.
- Treat any sequence change or removal of bracing/props as a design change until the designer confirms otherwise.
- Check the full load path, including existing structure that will take redistributed load.

Educational only — not for construction. Subject to the project temporary works procedure.

https://www.temporaryworksconsulting.com/news.html

#TemporaryWorks #BS5975 #StructuralStability #CDM2015 #TWC

body.p: On Wednesday 21 October 2026 a partial collapse involving a building under construction and associated scaffolding occurred on Lower Cherwell Street in Banbury, Oxfordshire. The site is the redevelopment of a former car sales premises into 19 apartments. Thames Valley Police stated that nine workers were on site; two sustained injuries and were taken to hospital (one with head and leg injuries, one described as severe). There were no reports of anyone trapped. HSE confirmed it is aware of the incident and an investigation is underway. No cause has been established in the published reports.

body.h: Why this is a temporary works prompt
body.p: Until the permanent structure is self-stable, construction sequence, temporary bracing, propping, scaffolding interfaces and any alteration to the load path are temporary works. HSE guidance on structural stability during alteration, demolition and dismantling states that temporary supports must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads, and that structures should never be overloaded. Items that affect stability belong on the Temporary Works Register under the project procedure (BS 5975-1:2024).

CROSS-UK Report 1479 (published 13 January 2026) describes a late contractor change on a filler-beam bridge deck. Instead of lifting steel beams in connected pairs, beams were to be lifted individually. This introduced a significant temporary stability risk of lateral-torsional buckling under the weight of wet concrete. Assessment showed utilisation exceeding 200% without rotational restraint and temporary LTB restraints. The Category II checker identified the issue; temporary restraints were required. The report notes that late changes to construction sequence can introduce significant temporary stability risks and that the Temporary Works Coordinator role must ensure clarity of design responsibility at each stage.

Build UK has announced that Version 6 of the Common Assessment Standard takes effect on 1 November 2026. Revisions to the Building Safety section reflect that scaffolding and temporary works no longer fall within the scope of the Building Safety Regulations unless they form part of the completed structure. NASC welcomed the clarification after seeking confirmation from MHCLG. Companies will opt out of the Building Safety section where it does not apply, with a confirming statement. Competence-based questions previously in Section 7 move into the quality section so they remain required. This does not remove the need for competence or for the procedural controls in BS 5975 and CDM 2015.

body.h: What a competent TWC / site team should confirm this week
ul: Every item that can affect structural stability during construction (scaffolding that is load-bearing or tied in a way that affects the permanent structure, temporary bracing, propping, sequence-critical elements) is on the Temporary Works Register with a named Temporary Works Coordinator.
There is a design or documented standard solution, an appropriate design check, a permit-to-load/use and a recent inspection by a person competent for that item.

Any proposed change to sequence, removal of bracing or props, or alteration of loading is treated as a design change and is not implemented until the temporary works designer confirms the temporary condition remains acceptable.
The full load path has been considered, including existing structure that will carry redistributed load (see also CROSS-UK Report 1539).
